title: One Shelf, Many Stories
passage: Every Tuesday after school, a small group of students at Midori Junior High met in the library. They were not there to study for a test. Instead, they had started a project called One Shelf, Many Stories. The idea came from Aya, who noticed that many students always borrowed the same popular books while other books stayed untouched for months. She wondered if those quiet books simply needed someone to introduce them. At first, the group made simple recommendation cards. Each card had a short summary, one sentence about why the book was interesting, and a small drawing. They placed the cards beside books that were rarely borrowed. During the first week, only a few students stopped to read them. The group felt a little disappointed, but the librarian told them not to give up. She suggested changing the cards every week so that students would have a reason to look again. The group then tried a new idea. Instead of writing only about the story, they connected each book to an everyday question. A book about a mountain climber had a card asking what a reader would do when facing a difficult decision alone. A science book about insects asked why tiny creatures sometimes survive where larger animals cannot. These questions made students curious. By the end of the month, the borrowing record had changed. Several books that had not been borrowed for a long time were taken home. More importantly, students began talking about the books with one another. Some even wrote their own recommendation cards and left them at the library desk. Aya realized that the project was not really about making old books popular. It was about giving people a small reason to notice something they had passed many times before. The books had always been there. What changed was the way students looked at them. The group also learned that small changes in presentation can affect attention. A bright card alone was not enough; a question that connected a book to a reader's own life worked better. By spring, students from another grade were asking how they could help. The project had begun with one shelf, but it slowly became a shared activity for the whole school.
translation: 毎週火曜日の放課後、緑中学校の少人数の生徒たちは図書館に集まっていました。テスト勉強のためではなく、『一つの棚、たくさんの物語』という活動を始めたのです。きっかけは彩でした。人気の本ばかりが借りられ、何か月も手に取られない本があることに気づき、それらは誰かが紹介してくれれば読まれるのではないかと考えました。最初は、短いあらすじ、おもしろいと思った理由、小さな絵を書いた紹介カードを作りました。しかし最初の一週間は、立ち止まる生徒はわずかでした。司書から毎週カードを替えてみるよう助言され、グループは工夫を始めます。物語の説明だけでなく、『一人で難しい決断をしなければならないとしたら？』など、日常につながる問いを添えることにしました。すると生徒たちは興味を持ち始め、長く借りられていなかった本も持ち帰られるようになりました。さらに、生徒同士で本について話し、自分で紹介カードを書く人まで現れました。彩は、この活動の本当の目的は古い本を人気にすることではなく、何度も通り過ぎていたものに気づく小さなきっかけを作ることだと理解します。本は最初からそこにあり、変わったのは見る側の視点でした。また、目立つカードだけでは十分ではなく、読者自身の生活と結びつく問いの方が注意を引くことも学びました。春には別の学年の生徒も参加を希望し、一つの棚から始まった活動は学校全体の共有活動へと広がっていきました。

title: Marks by the River
passage: Ken's grandfather lived near a river that ran through a farming town. When Ken was younger, he thought the river was simply a place where people fished, walked, or watched birds. During one summer visit, however, his grandfather showed him something Ken had never noticed before: small marks painted on several bridges and walls near the water. His grandfather explained that the marks showed how high the water had risen during past floods. Some were low, but one was far above Ken's head. The river looked calm that day, so it was difficult for him to imagine water reaching so high. The next morning, they walked along the river again. This time, Ken looked for signs of flood protection. He saw wide open spaces beside the river, strong walls, and paths that could also be used by emergency vehicles. His grandfather explained that some fields near the river were designed to hold extra water during heavy rain. A town could not stop every natural disaster, he said, but it could prepare. Ken became interested and asked why the old flood marks had not been removed. His grandfather answered that the marks were part of the town's memory. New technology could warn people about dangerous weather, but old signs could also teach important lessons. If people forgot what had happened before, they might believe that a calm river could never become dangerous. When Ken returned home, he made a short presentation for his class. He used photos of the flood marks and explained what he had learned. One classmate said there was a similar mark near her home, but she had never known what it meant. Another student decided to ask his family about past disasters in their area. Ken's teacher then asked the class to walk around their own neighborhoods and look for objects connected with safety. Students found evacuation signs, raised storage areas, and old maps showing places where water had once collected. Ken had expected his summer visit to be quiet. Instead, it changed the way he saw familiar places. He learned that a town can carry its history in ordinary objects. A line on a wall or an old sign may look unimportant, but it can help people understand risks and make better choices in the future.
translation: 健の祖父は、農村を流れる川の近くに住んでいました。幼いころの健にとって、川は釣りをしたり歩いたり鳥を見たりする場所にすぎませんでした。ところが夏に訪れたとき、祖父は橋や川沿いの壁に残る小さな印を見せました。それは過去の洪水で水がどこまで上がったかを示す印でした。中には健の頭よりはるかに高い位置にあるものもあり、穏やかな川からは想像できませんでした。翌朝、今度は洪水への備えを意識して歩くと、広い空き地、丈夫な壁、緊急車両も使える道などが見えてきました。川沿いの一部の土地は大雨のときに余分な水を受け止める役割もあると祖父は説明します。自然災害を完全に止めることはできなくても、備えることはできます。古い洪水の印を消さないのは、それが町の記憶だからでした。新しい技術による警報だけでなく、過去の痕跡も大切な教訓になります。帰宅後、健は写真を使ってクラスで発表しました。すると、家の近くにも似た印があるという生徒や、家族に昔の災害について聞いてみようという生徒が現れました。先生はさらに、自分の地域で安全に関係するものを探す課題を出しました。避難標識、高い位置の保管場所、昔水がたまった場所を示す地図などが見つかりました。健は、町の歴史は特別な資料館だけでなく、壁の線や古い看板のような普通のものにも残っていると学びました。それらは将来の危険を理解し、よりよい判断をする助けになるのです。

title: The One-Minute Habit
passage: Mika wanted to improve her English speaking, but she did not enjoy practicing long speeches. She often stopped because she worried about making mistakes. One day, her teacher suggested a different method: speak for only one minute about something nearby. At first, Mika thought the task was too easy. The teacher told her to choose any object, such as a pencil case, a plant, or a school bag, and explain what she noticed. The goal was not to use difficult words. The goal was to keep speaking, even when she had to change her sentence. Mika began with her water bottle. She described its color, where she bought it, and why she carried it every day. She made several grammar mistakes, but she finished the full minute. The next day, she spoke about the view from her classroom window. After a week, she noticed that she was pausing less. Then Mika added a new rule. After speaking, she wrote down one word or expression that she had wanted to use but did not know. She looked it up later and tried to use it the next day. This made her practice more useful because the new words came from things she actually wanted to say. A month later, her class had a short discussion activity. In the past, Mika had usually waited for other students to speak first. This time, she raised her hand. Her answer was not perfect, but she was able to explain her idea without becoming silent. Mika understood that her improvement had not come from one long practice session. It had come from many short attempts that felt safe enough to repeat. She still wanted to study grammar and learn more vocabulary, but she no longer believed she had to be fully prepared before speaking. Her one-minute habit also changed her attitude toward mistakes. A mistake was no longer proof that she could not speak English. It was information about what to practice next. Soon, two friends joined her, and they took turns choosing daily topics. Sometimes they laughed at unusual sentences, but they corrected each other kindly and continued. The small routine gave Mika something more valuable than perfect sentences: confidence built through repetition and the feeling that speaking was a skill she could train a little every day.
translation: 美香は英語を話す力を伸ばしたいと思っていましたが、長いスピーチ練習は苦手でした。間違いを気にして途中で止まってしまうからです。そこで先生は、身近なものについて一分だけ話す方法を勧めました。難しい単語を使うことではなく、言い直しながらでも話し続けることが目標です。美香はまず水筒について、色、買った場所、毎日持ち歩く理由を話しました。文法の間違いはありましたが、一分間話し切ることができました。翌日は教室の窓から見える景色について話し、一週間後には止まる回数が減っていることに気づきます。さらに、話したあと『言いたかったけれど知らなかった表現』を一つ書き留め、後で調べて翌日に使うというルールを加えました。自分が本当に言いたかった内容から新しい表現を学べるため、練習がより実用的になりました。一か月後のクラス討論では、以前なら他の人が話すのを待っていた美香が自分から手を挙げました。完璧ではなくても、黙り込まず考えを説明できました。上達は一度の長時間練習ではなく、繰り返せる小さな挑戦から生まれたのだと気づきます。間違いも『自分は話せない証拠』ではなく、『次に練習すべきことを教える情報』だと考えられるようになりました。やがて友人二人も加わり、毎日テーマを交代で決めました。おかしな文に笑うことがあっても、互いにやさしく直しながら続けました。この一分習慣が美香に与えたのは、完璧な英文よりも、反復から生まれる自信と、話す力は毎日少しずつ鍛えられるという実感でした。

title: The Bakery's Last Hour
passage: On Saturday mornings, a bakery near Sota's house sold bread at a lower price just before closing. Sota had always thought the bakery was simply trying to sell everything before the food became old. One day, however, he saw a poster explaining that the shop was also working to reduce food waste. Sota became curious and asked the owner how much bread was usually left at the end of the day. The owner said that the amount changed depending on the weather, holidays, and local events. If the shop made too little bread, customers were disappointed. If it made too much, some bread remained unsold. The bakery had tried several ways to solve the problem. First, the staff kept detailed records of sales. They learned that rainy afternoons usually meant fewer customers, while school events could suddenly increase demand. Second, they made smaller amounts of some products and baked additional bread later when necessary. Finally, they offered discount bags near closing time. Sota asked whether discounts caused people to wait until the end of the day instead of buying bread at the normal price. The owner said this sometimes happened, but not often enough to create a serious problem. Most customers wanted a particular kind of bread at a convenient time. The discount bags contained whatever was left, so buyers could not choose everything. For a school project, Sota compared this system with food waste at home. He realized that families also had to make small predictions: how much rice to cook, which vegetables to use first, and when to freeze extra food. His family started writing the date on containers and placing older food at the front of the refrigerator. After two weeks, they checked their trash and noticed that they were throwing away much less food. Sota also learned that reducing waste did not always require a large new machine or an expensive service. Better information and a few flexible habits could make a difference. The bakery had taught him that waste is often connected with uncertainty about the future, and careful records can help people make better everyday decisions.
translation: 颯太の家の近くのパン屋では、土曜日の閉店前になるとパンを安く売っていました。颯太は、古くなる前に売り切りたいだけだと思っていましたが、ある日、食品ロス削減の取り組みだと書かれたポスターを見つけます。店主に尋ねると、売れ残る量は天気、休日、地域行事によって大きく変わることが分かりました。少なく作れば買えない客が出て、多く作れば余ってしまいます。そこで店は、販売記録を細かく残し、雨の日は客が減ることや学校行事の日は需要が増えることを学びました。また、一度に作る量を減らし、必要なら後から追加で焼くようにしました。閉店前の割引袋もその工夫の一つです。割引を待つ客が増えないかと颯太が尋ねると、多少はいても大きな問題ではなく、多くの客は好きなパンを都合のよい時間に買いたいのだと店主は説明しました。割引袋は残ったパンの組み合わせなので、自由に選べないからです。学校の課題で颯太は家庭の食品ロスにも目を向けました。ご飯をどれだけ炊くか、どの野菜を先に使うか、余った物をいつ冷凍するかも小さな予測です。家族は容器に日付を書き、古い食品を冷蔵庫の手前に置くようにしました。二週間後、捨てる食品は明らかに減っていました。颯太は、食品ロスを減らすのに大きな機械や高価なサービスが必ずしも必要ではなく、情報と柔軟な習慣が役立つと学びます。無駄は未来を正確に予測できないことから生まれる場合があり、丁寧な記録が日々の判断を助けるのです。

title: What Must Be Ours
passage: When Yui's class planned a school festival, everyone wanted the classroom to look exciting. Some students suggested buying many decorations. Others wanted to build everything by hand. The class had only a small budget, so they needed a plan that would make the room attractive without spending too much money. Yui suggested borrowing materials from other classes and using things that were already available at school. At first, some classmates thought borrowed decorations would make their room look less original. Yui asked them to list what they truly needed to create themselves and what could be shared. The class decided that the main sign and game materials should be original because those things represented their idea. However, tables, lights, cloth, and storage boxes did not need to be unique. They borrowed some items from the art club and others from a class that was holding its event on a different floor. This created a new problem. The students had to keep track of who owned each item. Yui made small labels and a simple checklist. Each borrowed object had a number, the owner's name, and the place where it should be returned. The system seemed unnecessary at first, but it became useful when the festival ended and everyone was tired. After cleaning the room, the class returned every borrowed item. They had spent less than half of their original budget and still had enough money to replace a broken game part during the festival. Their teacher asked what they had learned. One student said the best idea was not a decoration itself but the decision to separate what must be ours from what only needs to work. Yui agreed. A week later, another class asked to borrow the labels and checklist for a sports event. Yui was pleased because even the management system could be shared. She realized that originality does not mean creating every object from zero. Sometimes a project becomes stronger when people save their effort for the parts that carry the main idea and share ordinary tools for the rest. The classroom looked colorful, but the most useful lesson was about choosing carefully where to put time, money, and energy.
translation: 結衣のクラスが文化祭を計画したとき、みんな教室を楽しく見せたいと考えました。飾りをたくさん買う案も、すべて手作りする案も出ましたが、予算は限られていました。そこで結衣は、他のクラスから借りたり、学校にすでにある物を使ったりすることを提案します。『借り物では独自性がなくなる』という声に対し、結衣は『自分たちで作る必要がある物』と『共有してもよい物』を分けて考えるよう促しました。メインの看板やゲーム道具は自分たちの考えを表すのでオリジナルにし、机、照明、布、収納箱などは借りることにしました。すると次に、誰の物か分からなくなる問題が出ます。結衣は番号、持ち主、返却場所を書いた小さなラベルとチェックリストを作りました。最初は面倒に見えた仕組みでしたが、文化祭終了後、疲れている中で片づけるときに大いに役立ち、すべて正しく返却できました。費用も当初予算の半分以下に抑えられ、途中で壊れたゲーム部品を買い直す余裕も残りました。先生に学んだことを聞かれた生徒は、『自分たちの物である必要がある部分と、機能すればよい部分を分けたこと』が最も大切だったと答えました。後日、別のクラスがスポーツ行事のためにそのラベルとチェックリストを借りに来ました。結衣は、管理の仕組みまで共有できることに気づきます。独自性とは何もかもゼロから作ることではなく、中心となる部分に力を集中し、普通の道具は共有することで、よりよい活動にできるのだと学びました。

title: The Same Camera
passage: Daichi used to believe that taking good photographs required an expensive camera. He enjoyed looking at travel photos online and often compared them with pictures from his phone. His own photos seemed ordinary, so he assumed the device was the problem. During a family trip, Daichi's aunt, who enjoyed photography, asked to use his phone for a few minutes. She took pictures of the same park that Daichi had photographed earlier. When they compared the images, Daichi was surprised. Her photos looked more interesting even though she had used exactly the same phone. His aunt explained that she usually thought about three things before pressing the button. First, she looked at the direction of the light. Second, she decided what the main subject was. Third, she checked the edges of the picture for objects that might distract the viewer. They practiced together. Instead of photographing an entire garden, Daichi chose one bench with yellow leaves around it. He moved a few steps to avoid a trash can in the background. Then he waited until a cloud changed the light. The result was much better than his first photo. After returning home, Daichi continued practicing with ordinary places. He photographed his bicycle, a cup on the kitchen table, and the path to school. Because the subjects were familiar, he could focus on composition rather than searching for something unusual. A few weeks later, he looked at his older photographs again. He noticed that many of them did not have a clear subject. He had often tried to include everything he could see. His newer pictures were simpler. He started printing one photo each week and writing a short note about the choice that had improved it. Sometimes the note was about light; sometimes it was about moving closer or waiting for a person to leave the background. Daichi still hoped to buy a better camera someday, but he no longer believed equipment alone would solve his problem. A tool could improve image quality, yet it could not decide where to stand, what to include, or when to wait. Those choices belonged to the person taking the picture. Learning to notice light, space, and unnecessary details had improved his photography more than buying a new device would have.
translation: 大地は以前、よい写真を撮るには高価なカメラが必要だと思っていました。旅行写真を見ては自分のスマートフォン写真と比べ、平凡に見える原因は機材だと考えていたのです。家族旅行のとき、写真好きの叔母が大地のスマートフォンで同じ公園を撮りました。すると、同じ機器なのに叔母の写真の方がずっと魅力的でした。叔母は、撮る前に三つ考えると言います。光の向き、主役となるもの、そして写真の端に邪魔な物が入っていないかです。二人は一緒に練習しました。庭全体を撮る代わりに黄色い葉に囲まれたベンチを主役にし、背景のごみ箱が入らないよう数歩動き、雲によって光が変わるのを待ちました。帰宅後も大地は、自転車、台所のカップ、通学路など身近な物を撮り続けました。見慣れた対象だからこそ、珍しい場所探しではなく構図に集中できました。数週間後、昔の写真を見ると、何でも画面に入れようとして主役が分からなくなっていたことに気づきます。そこで毎週一枚を印刷し、何を工夫したか短いメモを書くようにしました。光についての週もあれば、近づいたことや背景から人がいなくなるまで待ったことを書く週もありました。大地はいつか良いカメラを買いたいとは思っていますが、機材だけで問題が解決するとは考えなくなりました。画質は道具で向上しても、どこに立つか、何を入れるか、いつ待つかを決めるのは撮影する人です。光や空間、不要なものに気づく力こそが、機材購入以上に写真を上達させたのでした。
